doc.title: Ray Blue interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 23, 2022

title: Recording Sweet Emma and Everything Happens to Me
summary: Blue discusses Sweet Emma, and the sax-and-drums opening of Everything Happens to Me with drummer Steve Johns.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: I was happy to see that you recorded [scats]

Yes, “Sweet Emma.” It was, yeah, that’s another great tune and there’s a story behind it that’s great as well, because Emma was one of those persons who, a woman in the man’s world who made her presence, it was something else. And she not only is a great player but a dynamic personality. That song was written about her. You know? And so yeah, it had a strong sassy swing thing to it, and Nat [Adderley] did a great job.
He did. This may not seem like a big deal but you recorded “Everything Happens to Me.” And the whole first statement of the melody it’s just you and the drums. Am I correct?

To me that is such a terrific thing to do and not many people if they even think of doing it they wouldn’t do it anyway. And I think it’s worth noting from an arranger’s standpoint that within a quartet you’ve got all these possibilities of combinations. So I just wanted to say I’m glad you did it.

Well thank you. Thank you. It’s one of those things that happened. You know we plan for things and this was just one that we said you know, let’s try this. I want to try this. So we did it. And Steve Johns, who was on the drum track on that, Steve is an amazing cat to work with in the studio you know. His studio skills are second to none, really. He’s a great cat playing live with but in the studio his experience and knowledge and the way he connects, I keep using that word but it’s really a relevant term. The way he connects with me, or the person that’s doing the lead, he’s right there. He’s right there. You know? And he’s sensitive to each breath I take. He feels the emotion, where it’s leading. He speaks very well and supports — he’s a great musician you know.
Yes and in the studio, it’s interesting you mention that because sometimes we can be separated, the drummer might be in a booth or something so they really have to be tuned in from their ears.
In that particular case he was in the room next to me and we could see one another.
Yeah. And that worked too so we — so that’s the deal. That’s how that came about.
